lessons.title: Daily checks, feeding and water
lessons.html:
Daily checks, feeding and water

Production depends on the daily routine being done properly. This module covers the hands-on practices that keep animals growing, breeding and producing.

The daily round

  • Count the animals in each camp and compare with the register.
  • Check every water point: is water flowing, is the trough clean, is the float valve working, is the reservoir full?
  • Check lick troughs: is there enough, is it dry, are animals eating the expected amount?
  • Look for sick, injured, lame or missing animals.
  • Check fences and gates.
  • Look out for signs of predators or stock theft: tracks, cut fences, carcasses.
  • Record what you find and report problems the same day.

Feeding in pens and feedlots

When animals are fed in pens, feed at the same times every day. Check bunks before feeding: empty bunks mean animals are hungry; lots of leftovers mean they are sick or the feed is bad. Change rations gradually over several days to prevent acidosis and bloat. Keep feed dry and free of mould, and store it away from rats.

Licks

Put out the lick the farm uses for the season. Follow the supplier's instructions on intake. Licks that contain urea are dangerous if animals eat too much at once, especially hungry animals or animals that have not been introduced to it. Keep lick dry; wet urea licks can become toxic.

Water quality

Clean troughs regularly to remove algae, dead birds and dung. Report water that smells, has a colour or that animals refuse to drink. In summer, cattle and sheep drink much more, so check water more often on hot days.

lessons.title: Breeding, birth and young animals
lessons.html:
Breeding, birth and young animals

The breeding season

Help to put bulls or rams in with the females on the planned date, and take them out on time. Check rams' marking harnesses and change crayon colours as instructed so the farm knows when each ewe was served. Watch bulls for lameness or injury - a bull that cannot serve means empty cows.

Watching for heat

A cow on heat stands still to be mounted by others. She may be restless and have clear mucus from the vulva. Record the tag number and time and tell the supervisor, especially on farms that use artificial insemination.

Births

Check pregnant females often during the season, at least morning and evening. Most births are normal. Call your supervisor if:

  • The female has strained for a long time with no progress.
  • Only one leg, only the head, or the tail appears.
  • The young is born weak or not breathing.
  • The afterbirth has not come out after a long time.

Never pull hard or use a vehicle to pull a calf. Wear gloves when touching afterbirths and wash your hands.

The newborn

  1. Check that the young is breathing and clear mucus from the nose.
  2. Make sure it suckles colostrum within the first hours.
  3. Treat the navel as the farm instructs.
  4. Tag or mark it and record dam, date and sex.
  5. Protect it from cold, wet wind and predators.

Weaning

On weaning day, separate the young from the mothers calmly, weigh them if the farm does so, and keep them in a good camp with clean water and feed. Fence-line weaning, where mothers and young can see each other through a fence, reduces stress.

lessons.title: Routine procedures and production records
lessons.html:
Routine procedures and production records

Marking and identification

Ear tags must be placed in the correct position in the ear, between the ribs of cartilage and away from blood vessels, using a clean applicator. Tattoos and brands must follow the registered marks of the farm. Record each animal's number in the register.

Other procedures

Castration, dehorning, tail docking and hoof trimming must be done at the age, with the method and with the pain relief the farm and vet prescribe. Only do them when trained and supervised. Clean instruments between animals, and treat wounds against flies.

Weighing

Weigh animals calmly on a scale or use a weigh band where trained. Zero the scale first. Record the tag number and the weight clearly. Weights are used for dosing, for selection and to decide when to sell.

Shearing and wool

On sheep farms, help to keep the shed clean and dry, keep sheep off feed and water for the period the farm sets before shearing, and keep wool free of plastic, string and dung. Wool is sorted by type and must not be contaminated.

Milking

In a dairy, follow the milking routine: clean teats, check the first streams for clots, attach units correctly, dip teats after milking. Keep milk from treated cows out of the bulk tank.

Records

RecordWhy
Births and deathsHerd numbers and losses
WeightsGrowth, dosing, selling
TreatmentsFood safety and planning
Camp movesGrazing management

Key points

  • Count animals and check water and lick every round.
  • Change feed slowly; keep licks dry.
  • Call the supervisor for difficult births; never pull with a vehicle.
  • Every newborn must drink colostrum.
  • Record births, weights and treatments clearly.
